podaccess:item.itunes:title: Anthropic goes to Wall Street
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Anthropic has just gone public in the biggest IPO in history. After a lot of toing-and-froing over its valuation, investors eventually priced the firm at $1.3trn at the end of its first day of trading. What does that mean for Wall Street—and for the future of AI?


Guests and hosts:

  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Miles Kruppa, technology correspondent at The Economist


Topics covered:

  • Anthropic’s IPO
  • Nvidia
  • Dario Amodei

podaccess:item.itunes:title: How to prepare for an AI world
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
The AI industry has been shaken in the past week. First, investors—rattled by the success of anti-data centre Democrats in the midterms—sent tech stocks tumbling. Then came the scandal surrounding Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. We wanted to know what to make of all that, and how to prepare for an AI world, so we spoke to Gina Raimondo. She was commerce secretary when ChatGPT was launched and she has now built a foundation to deal with the impact AI might have on workers.


Guests and hosts:

  • Gina Raimondo, former US Secretary of Commerce and CEO of RAISE US
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • AI retraining
  • Data centres
  • Jensen Huang scandal

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Why big law has big problems
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
The legal industry is losing one of its best-known firms. Weil, Gotshal & Manges is the first major victim of changes that are gripping what was, until recently, a staid profession. But the emergence of superstar partners, paid tens of millions of dollars, and the adoption of AI are changing that stuffy reputation. How much trouble is big law really in?


Guests and hosts:

  • John Pottow, University of Michigan
  • Max Junestrand, CEO of Legora
  • Shera Avi-Yonah, The Economist’s business correspondent
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Weil, Gotshal & Manges
  • Legal profession
  • AI

It's Mike's last show. And there was only one thing he wanted to talk about: the biggest story on his beat. He speaks to legendary distressed debt investor Howard Marks about the AI boom and the risks of a blow-up.

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Sam Bankman-Fried on effective altruism
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Sam Bankman-Fried was the poster child for effective altruism. Before his arrest, he had done more than anyone to promote the movement. Today, no one has done more damage. Yet, in Silicon Valley, EAs (as adherents are known) are everywhere. Should you worry that a philosophy that inspired the man behind one of America’s largest frauds has taken root in the world’s most important firms? We ask Bankman-Fried himself. We also speak to one of the founding fathers of the EA movement.


Guests and hosts:

  • Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of FTX
  • Toby Ord, co-founder of Giving What We Can
  • Shera Avi-Yonah, The Economist’s US business correspondent
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Effective Altruism
  • AI
  • Silicon Valley

podaccess:item.itunes:title: A Nobel-winning economics lesson
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
It’s that time of year again. An economist gets a call from Sweden–and we then badger them to speak to us. We’re pleased to say Michael Woodford, who shared the award with Robert Hall, returned our call. The prize committee credited the duo with rebuilding macroeconomics on “microfoundations”: representing economic outcomes as the result of the behaviour of individuals and businesses. On this week’s show, Mr Woodford explains his theory.


Guests and hosts:

  • Michael Woodford, Columbia University
  • Henry Curr, The Economist’s acting business affairs editor
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Nobel prize for economics
  • Economic theory
  • New Keynesian economics

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Are populists wrecking your portfolio?
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Investors have a big problem. Their sharpest tool, diversification, is getting blunter. And one possible culprit may surprise you: Donald Trump. A growing number of investors blame populist politicians for upending the world order and ruining the logic behind their most important strategies. Are they right?


Guests and hosts:

  • Ed Cole, of Man Group
  • Josh Roberts, The Economist’s acting Britain editor
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Populism
  • Investment strategies
  • Inflation

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Big booze is reinventing itself
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Global alcohol consumption fell by 2% in 2025. It was the third straight year of decline, as younger drinkers prove they are not as boozy as their parents. As drinks-makers face an uncertain future, competition is sharpening. With brewers, vintners and distillers expanding into new domains, which companies hold the advantage?


Guests and hosts:

  • Jacob Aarup-Andersen, CEO of Carlsberg
  • Trevor Stirling, analyst at Bernstein
  • Avantika Chilkoti, global business writer at The Economist
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Alcoholic drinks industry
  • Ready-to-drink cocktails

podaccess:item.itunes:title: The great global bond sell-off
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
The global bond sell-off is deepening. This week, the yield on ten-year American Treasuries surpassed 5%, its highest level in two decades. Meanwhile British gilts, German bunds and Japanese government bonds are all soaring to multi-year highs. Investors are under pressure from persistent inflation, government debt and the AI borrowing binge. We ask whether high long-term yields are here to stay.


Guests and hosts:

  • Mark Dowding, Chief Investment Officer for BlueBay fixed income
  • Mike Bird, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Bond markets
  • Scott Bessent
  • AI infrastructure buildout

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Why the AI giants are acting like banks
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Since 2022, the AI boom has been the biggest story in financial markets. It has turned some of the largest tech companies into major financial players, lending and borrowing from one another. This week, we dig into how worried you should be about that web of “circular” AI financing.


Guests and hosts:

  • Shailesh Chitnis, The Economist's global business writer 
  • Mike Bird, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Nvidia
  • AI boom
  • “Circular” financing

podaccess:item.itunes:title: A long weekend in Jackson Hole
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Each August, the world’s central bankers descend on Jackson Hole. Normally, the coffee-break chatter is about policy. But this year, the big question was what Kevin Warsh, the enigmatic new Fed Chair, was really thinking—about how the Fed works, its independence and monetary policy. His speech was surprisingly revealing. Our acting economics editor tells us what he learned.


Guests and hosts:

  • Archie Hall, The Economist’s acting economics editor
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • Kevin Warsh

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Should investors stop buying American?
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
For decades, America’s stock exchanges have been the destination of choice for international investors. And no wonder, since that is where the Magnificent Seven tech firms are listed. Until recently these behemoths were generating gushing streams of cash, spending little of it and delivering stellar returns. But are they—and the rest of America’s stock market—now losing their shine?


Guests and hosts:

  • Michael Hartnett, Bank of America investment strategist
  • Josh Roberts, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”

podaccess:item.itunes:summary:

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Investors want to change how babies are made
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Humans have, mostly, made babies the same way for millenia. That kind of inertia is catnip to Silicon Valley investors who are pouring money into technology like embryo screening. On this week’s show, we explore the companies offering fertility tech and hear why some don’t shy away from terms like eugenics.

podaccess:item.itunes:title: A report card for Kevin Warsh
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Conspiracy theories were rife when Kevin Warsh was made Fed chair. Was he a hawk in dove's clothing or a dove dressed as a hawk? The tinfoil hats came out because Mr Warsh himself remained tight-lipped. Now, though, he has presided over two rate-setting meetings at the Fed. So what have we learnt about the world’s most important central banker?


Guests and hosts:

  • Josh Roberts, The Economist’s capital markets correspondent
  • Archie Hall, The Economist’s acting economics editor
  • Alex Domash, The Economist’s acting US economics editor

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Why economists love burgers
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
Travelling for work is rarely glamorous. And nowhere is that more true than at The Economist. Our correspondents have spent the last four decades travelling the world, expensing Big Macs in service of one aim: to understand how currencies work. To celebrate the Big Mac index’s 40th birthday, we share what we’ve learnt.

podaccess:item.itunes:title: Will the data-centre backlash derail the AI boom?
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
America’s AI giants have a problem. The likes of Google, Meta and Microsoft want to spend $3trn on data centres over the next four years. But a backlash among Americans, who don’t want sheds full of chips humming away near their backyards, has made it difficult to find a spot to build them. Will that slow the AI race?

podaccess:item.itunes:title: How quickly could you burn through $2.4trn?
podaccess:item.itunes:summary:
For America's social security trust fund, the answer is around six years. A growing elderly population and falling birth rate mean the pot, accumulated over decades will run dry some time towards the end of the next presidential term, in late 2032. When that happens, the country's retirees will take a battering. So can anything be done to stop it before time runs out?


Hosts:

  • Mike Bird, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Alice Fulwood, co-host of “Money Talks”
  • Ethan Wu, co-host of “Money Talks”


Topics covered:

  • America’s Social Security Trust Fund
